definition: Quick to notice and understand things that are not obvious.
example: The perspicacious editor noticed that the two sources shared the same original error.
nuance: Perspicacious emphasizes penetrating insight; it is more specific than simply intelligent.
prompt: A reviewer spots a hidden assumption that everyone else has missed.
options: Her perspicacious analysis exposed the assumption beneath the argument.
His perspicacious memory let him recite the report word for word.
The perspicacious speaker persuaded the audience through sheer charisma.
The reviewer called the essay perspicacious simply because its short sentences were easy to follow.
reasons: This sentence demonstrates the meaning: quick to notice and understand things that are not obvious.
Memory alone does not establish perceptive understanding.
Charisma and persuasion do not necessarily involve insight.
Easy-to-follow writing is perspicuous; perspicacious describes a perceptive mind, not clear prose.

practice.prompt: A museum guide studies a painting that was recently donated to the collection.
options: The perspicacious guide walked right past the large water stain across the corner.
The perspicacious guide declared the painting genuine without bothering to examine it.
The perspicacious guide spoke so loudly that visitors in the next gallery could hear.
The perspicacious guide realized the frame was decades newer than the canvas it held.
reasons: Missing a big, plain flaw is the reverse of keen perception.
Confident claims made without looking show certainty, not insight.
A loud voice has nothing to do with noticing or understanding things.
Spotting a subtle mismatch that most people would overlook shows sharp insight.
